A kitchen relocation requires a builder (for structural work), a plumber, a Gas Safe engineer (if gas is involved), an electrician and a kitchen installer. Coordinating all trades in the correct sequence is essential.

Trade Sequence for a Kitchen Relocation

  1. Structural work (builder) — openings, new floor structure if needed
  2. New plumbing supply and waste runs to the new location
  3. New electrical circuits run to the new location
  4. Gas Safe engineer relocates or extends the gas supply if needed
  5. Kitchen installation in the new room
  6. Making good the old kitchen location — plastering, flooring, decoration

The Drainage Challenge Most People Underestimate

Waste water needs a consistent fall to reach the existing drain run, and the further the new kitchen location is from the original waste stack, the harder this becomes — in some cases a macerator pump, similar to those used for downstairs toilets, is needed to move waste water uphill or over a long horizontal run.

What Happens to the Old Kitchen Space?

Once the kitchen moves out, the old space needs a new purpose and a full making-good — this typically includes capping off old services safely, replastering where units and pipework have been removed, and matching the flooring to whatever the new room's function will be.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to move a kitchen to a different room?
faqs.a: Moving a kitchen to a different room typically costs £5,000–£15,000 or more, depending on the scale of structural, plumbing and electrical work required.

faqs.q: Does moving a kitchen require planning permission?
faqs.a: Not usually, but if the work involves structural changes, an extension or changes to the external appearance of the property, planning permission or building regulations approval may be required.

faqs.q: How long does it take to move a kitchen?
faqs.a: A kitchen relocation project typically takes 3–6 weeks from start to completion, depending on the complexity of the structural, plumbing and electrical work involved.

title: What Is the Difference Between an Integrated and Freestanding Kitchen?
shortTitle: Difference Between Integrated and Freestanding Kitchens
metaDescription: Integrated kitchens have built-in appliances behind matching doors. Freestanding kitchens have standalone appliances. Find out the key differences.
answer: An integrated kitchen has appliances (fridge, dishwasher, oven, washing machine) built into the kitchen unit run, concealed behind matching cabinet doors. A freestanding kitchen uses standalone appliances that are not built into the cabinetry.
bodyHtml:
Integrated Kitchens

Integrated appliances are built into purpose-designed unit housings. The appliance door is either fixed to a matching kitchen door (door-on-door) or the door is integrated directly onto the appliance (fixed-door). The result is a seamless appearance where appliances are invisible within the kitchen run.

Freestanding Kitchens

Freestanding appliances stand independently and are not concealed within cabinetry. They are generally less expensive to purchase and replace, and offer more flexibility in kitchen layout. They are also easier to take with you if you move home.

Which Is Right for You?

  • Integrated kitchens offer a cleaner aesthetic and are preferred in modern, high-end kitchen designs
  • Freestanding appliances are more flexible, often cheaper and simpler to service and replace
  • Installation of integrated appliances is more complex and must be planned carefully at design stage

Integrated vs Freestanding: Side by Side

IntegratedFreestanding
AppearanceHidden behind matching doorsVisible appliance fascia
Upfront costHigherLower
Replacing the appliance laterMust match housing dimensions exactlyAny appliance of the right external size will do
Moving homeTypically stays with the propertyCan usually be taken with you
Installation complexityHigher — door fixing and alignmentLower — position and connect

A Practical Middle Ground

Some kitchens use a mix — an integrated dishwasher and fridge for a seamless look on the main run, with a freestanding range cooker as a deliberate feature. This is a common and practical compromise rather than an all-or-nothing decision.

What Happens When an Integrated Appliance Reaches End of Life?

Because replacement models change external dimensions over time, finding an exact match for an ageing integrated appliance's housing can be harder than replacing a freestanding one — worth factoring in if you plan to stay in the property long-term.

faqs.q: Does integrated kitchen installation cost more?
faqs.a: Yes. Integrated appliance fitting involves more complex housing assembly, door fixing and connection work than positioning freestanding appliances.

faqs.q: Can I convert a freestanding kitchen to integrated?
faqs.a: In some cases, yes — but it depends on whether the unit run has the correct housing units and whether the gap dimensions match the appliance. Discuss with your kitchen designer.

faqs.q: Do integrated appliances need more maintenance?
faqs.a: Not more maintenance, but accessing an integrated appliance for servicing can be more complex as the unit door and housing must be opened or removed.

title: Who Does the Gas Connection for a Kitchen?
metaDescription: Gas connections in a kitchen must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Find out what gas work is involved in a kitchen installation and who does it.
answer: Gas connections in a kitchen must be carried out by a Gas Safe registered engineer. This includes connecting a gas cooker or hob, extending or relocating a gas supply, and any work on the gas supply infrastructure.
bodyHtml:
What Gas Work Is Needed in a Kitchen

Kitchen gas work typically involves connecting a gas hob or range cooker to the gas supply, and sometimes relocating the gas supply point if the cooker position is changing. Any work involving the gas pipework or connections must be done by a Gas Safe registered engineer.

Kitchen Fitters and Gas

Most kitchen fitters are not Gas Safe registered and cannot legally connect gas appliances. Your kitchen fitter will typically position the gas cooker or hob but leave the final gas connection to a Gas Safe engineer who visits after the unit installation is complete.

Booking a Gas Safe Engineer

  • Book your Gas Safe engineer before your installation date — they may need to visit twice (first fix and connection)
  • Ensure the engineer knows what appliance is being connected and where the supply point is
  • Request a certificate on completion of the gas connection

Typical Sequence for a Gas Appliance

StageWhoWhat happens
First fixGas Safe engineerSupply pipe run or relocated to the new position
InstallationKitchen fitterHob or cooker positioned in the housing
ConnectionGas Safe engineerFinal connection, leak test, certificate issued

What If You're Switching From Electric to Gas (or Vice Versa)?

Changing fuel type for your cooker is more involved than a like-for-like swap — it may mean running an entirely new gas supply or, in the other direction, capping off an existing one and adding a dedicated electrical circuit. Flag this at survey stage so it's accounted for in your installation schedule and price.

Can You Use the Same Gas Safe Engineer as Your Plumber?

Only if they hold a current Gas Safe registration in addition to their plumbing qualifications — not all plumbers do. Always check the Gas Safe register directly rather than assuming a general plumber is qualified for gas work.

faqs.q: Can a kitchen fitter connect a gas hob?
faqs.a: Only if they are Gas Safe registered. Most kitchen fitters are not Gas Safe registered and cannot legally connect gas appliances.

faqs.q: How much does a Gas Safe engineer charge for a kitchen connection?
faqs.a: Gas Safe engineers typically charge £80–£200 for connecting a gas hob or cooker, depending on complexity and whether the supply point needs moving.

faqs.q: Do I get a certificate for gas connection?
faqs.a: Yes. A Gas Safe registered engineer must provide a certificate on completion of the gas connection work. Keep this for your records and for any future property sale.

title: How Do You Fit an Under-Counter Fridge?
metaDescription: Under-counter fridges can be freestanding, integrated or semi-integrated. Find out how each type is fitted and what the installation involves.
answer: An under-counter fridge is fitted by positioning it in the correct unit housing, ensuring adequate ventilation clearance, levelling it on the adjustable feet, and connecting it to the electrical supply. Integrated models have a matching kitchen door fixed to the appliance door.
bodyHtml:
Types of Under-Counter Fridge Installation

Freestanding under-counter fridges are simply positioned under the worktop and plugged in. Semi-integrated fridges have a kitchen door covering the top portion with the control panel exposed at the bottom. Fully integrated fridges are entirely concealed behind a matching kitchen door on a door-on-door or fixed-door hinge mechanism.

Key Installation Steps

  • Check ventilation clearance requirements — fridges need airflow around the body to operate efficiently
  • Level the appliance using the adjustable feet so the door seal is even
  • For integrated models, fix the kitchen door to the appliance door using the hinge kit supplied
  • Connect to the electrical supply — under-counter fridges use a standard 13A socket

Common Issues

The most common installation problem with under-counter fridges is insufficient ventilation clearance, which causes the fridge to run hot and inefficiently. Always check the manufacturer's ventilation requirements and allow the specified clearances.

Freestanding vs Semi-Integrated vs Fully Integrated

TypeInstallation effortAppearance
FreestandingLowest — position and plug inVisible appliance front
Semi-integratedModerate — door fixed to top portionPartially concealed, controls visible
Fully integratedHighest — door-on-door hinge fittingFully concealed behind matching door

Why Ventilation Clearance Is Non-Negotiable

An under-counter fridge fitted without the manufacturer's specified clearance will run its compressor harder and for longer to maintain temperature, shortening its working life and increasing running costs — this is one of the most common installation mistakes on integrated fridges, where a snug-looking fit is prioritised over the airflow gap the appliance actually needs.

What If the Housing Unit Doesn't Have a Ventilation Grille?

Some older or budget housing units lack a built-in vent at the plinth level. If yours doesn't, ask your fitter whether a vent can be added — a sealed housing with an integrated fridge inside can cause the appliance to overheat and underperform.

faqs.q: Does an integrated fridge need a special socket?
faqs.a: No — integrated fridges use a standard 13A socket positioned inside the unit housing. Your electrician should position the socket inside the housing during first fix.

faqs.q: Can I fit an under-counter fridge myself?
faqs.a: A freestanding under-counter fridge can be positioned by a homeowner. Integrated models with door-fixing mechanisms are more complex and are best handled by a kitchen fitter.

faqs.q: How much ventilation does an under-counter fridge need?
faqs.a: Most under-counter fridges require 25–50mm clearance at the back and sides. Check the specific requirements in your appliance manual.

title: What Is the Best Worktop for a Kitchen?
metaDescription: Find out the pros and cons of the most popular kitchen worktop materials and which is best for your needs.
answer: The best worktop depends on your budget, lifestyle and aesthetic preference. Quartz is the most popular premium choice for durability and low maintenance; laminate offers excellent value; solid wood adds warmth; granite is hard-wearing and unique.
bodyHtml:
Quartz Worktops

Engineered quartz (such as Silestone or Caesarstone) is extremely hard-wearing, non-porous and available in a wide range of colours and finishes. It does not require sealing and resists staining well. It is the most popular premium worktop choice in UK kitchens. Installation requires specialist templating and fitting — quartz cannot be cut on site.

Laminate Worktops

Laminate offers excellent value and has improved significantly in quality and appearance. It is cut on site, making it faster and cheaper to install. It is not as heat or scratch resistant as stone but is perfectly practical for everyday use.

Solid Wood Worktops

Solid wood adds warmth and character. It requires regular oiling to maintain and can be sanded and refinished if it shows wear over time. It is not ideal near the sink area due to moisture sensitivity.

Granite

Natural granite is extremely hard-wearing and each slab is unique. It requires periodic sealing and is installed in the same way as quartz — templating followed by a separate fitting visit.

Worktop Comparison at a Glance

MaterialDurabilityMaintenanceRelative cost
QuartzVery highNone — no sealing needed£300–£900 per linear metre
LaminateGood for everyday useMinimalLowest cost, cut on site
Solid woodModerate — shows wearRegular oilingMid-range
GraniteVery highPeriodic sealingComparable to quartz

A Consideration Often Missed: Sink Compatibility

Not every worktop material suits every sink style equally well — an undermount sink needs a worktop edge that can be polished and sealed cleanly (stone is ideal, laminate is not generally suitable for undermounting), while a Belfast sink's exposed apron works with almost any worktop material since it sits proud of the surface rather than beneath it.

Can You Mix Worktop Materials in One Kitchen?

Yes — a common approach is stone on the main run with a contrasting solid wood section on an island or breakfast bar, though this adds a second templating and fitting process and should be planned and quoted for as such from the outset.

faqs.q: How much does a quartz worktop cost?
faqs.a: Quartz worktops typically cost £300–£900 per linear metre installed, depending on the brand, thickness and edge profile chosen.

faqs.q: Is laminate worktop good quality?
faqs.a: Yes. Modern laminate worktops from reputable suppliers are practical, durable and good-looking. They offer the best cost-to-quality ratio for most kitchens.

faqs.q: Can kitchen worktops be replaced without replacing the units?
faqs.a: Yes. Worktops are fitted on top of the units and can be replaced independently. The units must be temporarily disconnected from the worktop and any upstand or splashback removed first.

title: Can I Replace a Kitchen Worktop Without Replacing Units?
metaDescription: Yes, kitchen worktops can be replaced without replacing the units. Find out how the process works and what it costs.
answer: Yes. Kitchen worktops can be replaced without changing the units. The old worktop is removed, the new one is measured, cut and fitted in its place. This is one of the most cost-effective ways to refresh a kitchen.
bodyHtml:
What the Process Involves

The sink is disconnected and lifted out. The old worktop is unfixed from the units (usually via clips or brackets underneath) and removed. Any upstand or splashback fixed to the wall at the worktop line is also removed. The new worktop is then measured, cut and fitted. The sink is refitted and reconnected.

Important Considerations

  • Stone worktops (quartz, granite) require a template visit before fabrication — the new slab cannot be cut until the units are confirmed in position
  • If the tiles or splashback behind the old worktop are different in height or colour from what was behind it, this may need re-tiling
  • The unit tops must be clean, level and sound for the new worktop to sit correctly

Cost Benefit

A new worktop can transform the look of a kitchen at a fraction of the cost of full replacement. If units are structurally sound and the layout works, worktop replacement alone can make a substantial visual difference.

What to Check Before Committing to Worktop-Only Replacement

  • Are the unit tops themselves flat, dry and structurally sound?
  • Is the existing sink cut-out a standard size that a new sink can reuse, or will it need re-cutting?
  • Is the tiled splashback height compatible with the new worktop thickness?
  • Are the units level — an uneven base will telegraph through a stone worktop over time

Worktop-Only Replacement Timeline

MaterialTypical timeline
LaminateRemoved and refitted in a single day
Quartz/graniteTemplate day 1, fabrication 7–14 days, fitting day

What If the Old Worktop Is Glued Down?

Some older laminate worktops were fixed with adhesive as well as brackets, which can make removal slower and occasionally risks minor damage to the unit tops beneath — your fitter should check the fixing method before quoting a worktop-only job so there are no surprises on the day.

faqs.q: How long does worktop replacement take?
faqs.a: Laminate worktop replacement can typically be completed in one day. Stone worktops require a template visit (day 1), fabrication (7–14 days), and a fitting day.

faqs.q: Does replacing a worktop require a plumber?
faqs.a: The sink connection and disconnection involves basic plumbing. Some kitchen fitters can handle this; others will advise you to book a plumber for the sink reconnection.

faqs.q: Can I keep my existing sink when replacing the worktop?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the sink is in good condition and the new worktop can be cut for the same sink cut-out dimensions.

title: How Do Kitchen Fitters Deal With Uneven Walls?
metaDescription: Uneven walls are common in older UK properties. Find out how professional kitchen fitters handle this challenge.
answer: Kitchen fitters deal with uneven walls by scribing panels and units to the wall profile, using filler pieces to close gaps, or packing units out from the wall where necessary. The goal is a clean, gap-free result regardless of the wall condition.
bodyHtml:
Scribing

Scribing is the primary technique for dealing with uneven walls. A panel, end panel or filler piece is held against the wall and a scribe line is drawn on it using a compass or scribing tool. The panel is then cut to that line and sits perfectly against the wall's actual surface.

Packing Out

Where a wall has a significant bulge in the centre but is flatter at the sides, units may be packed out from the wall to clear the bulge. This creates a gap between the back of the unit and the wall, which is then covered by the end panel or by a filler strip.

When Walls Need More Work

If walls are severely out of plumb (more than 20–25mm variation), plastering or dot-and-dab plasterboard may be needed before kitchen installation to create a workable surface. A thorough pre-installation survey will identify if this level of preparation is required.

Scribing vs Packing Out: When to Use Each

Wall conditionTechnique
Consistent slight leanScribe end panels to the wall profile
Bulge in the middle, flat at the endsPack units out from the wall to clear the bulge
Severely out of plumb (over ~20–25mm)Plaster or dot-and-dab before installation

Why This Matters More at the End of a Run

The end unit of a run against a wall is where uneven wall problems become most visible, since any gap has nowhere to hide behind an adjacent unit — this is why end panels are almost always scribed individually to the specific wall they meet, rather than cut to a standard size in advance.

Does Wall Unevenness Affect Tiling Later?

Yes, indirectly — if a wall is significantly out of plumb behind where a splashback will go, the tiler will need to account for this separately when setting the tile line, since kitchen unit scribing doesn't solve the wall condition above the worktop.

faqs.q: Are uneven walls common in UK kitchens?
faqs.a: Very common, particularly in Victorian, Edwardian and early post-war properties. Experienced kitchen fitters expect this and plan for it.

faqs.q: Will uneven walls affect the kitchen installation price?
faqs.a: Significantly uneven walls may add time to the installation and therefore cost. A good survey will identify this in advance so the quote accounts for it.

faqs.q: Does scribing take a long time?
faqs.a: Scribing a panel accurately takes 20–45 minutes. On a kitchen with multiple awkward wall junctions, scribing work can add half a day or more to the overall installation time.

title: What Is a Belfast Sink and How Is It Fitted?
metaDescription: Belfast sinks are heavy, traditional ceramic sinks that require special fitting. Find out how they are installed and what to consider.
answer: A Belfast sink is a large, deep ceramic sink with a traditional appearance, originally designed with an overflow at the front. It is heavier than a standard sink and requires a specially built or reinforced unit base to support it.
bodyHtml:
What Makes Belfast Sink Fitting Different

A Belfast sink is significantly heavier than a standard undermount or inset sink — typically 25–60kg depending on size. It must be supported on a dedicated base unit or custom-built support rather than simply resting on the worktop as a drop-in sink would. The worktop or unit front must be cut precisely to accept the sink apron.

Installation Steps

  • The base unit must be built or modified to provide solid support for the full weight of the sink
  • The worktop is cut to the correct depth to allow the sink to sit at the right height
  • The waste fitting and overflow (where applicable) are connected before the sink is positioned
  • Supply connections are made by a plumber after the sink is in place

Planning Considerations

Belfast sinks project further from the wall than standard sinks, which affects the worktop depth required. The waste position must also be planned carefully as the deep bowl creates a low outlet point. Discuss these requirements with your kitchen fitter and plumber at survey stage.

Belfast Sink vs Standard Inset Sink

Belfast sinkStandard inset sink
Weight25–60kgTypically under 10kg
Support neededReinforced or purpose-built base unitStandard worktop cut-out
Worktop depth impactSink projects forward, affecting depthSits flush within standard depth
Tap height neededTall or crosshead tap recommendedStandard tap height usually fine

Retrofitting a Belfast Sink Into an Existing Kitchen

Adding a Belfast sink to a kitchen that wasn't designed for one usually means replacing the base unit beneath it entirely, since standard cabinets rarely have the strength or the correct front cut-out — this is worth costing separately from a simple sink swap.

Do Belfast Sinks Need a Special Waste Kit?

Often yes — because the bowl sits lower and the front apron is exposed, standard waste kits designed for inset sinks may not give enough clearance underneath. Check the waste kit is specified for Belfast or butler sink installations.

faqs.q: Can any kitchen unit support a Belfast sink?
faqs.a: No. A Belfast sink requires a reinforced or purpose-designed base unit. Standard pre-assembled base units may not be strong enough without modification.

faqs.q: Do I need a special tap for a Belfast sink?
faqs.a: Not necessarily, but the deep bowl of a Belfast sink means that a standard tap height may be impractical. A tall or crosshead tap is often chosen to suit the sink's depth and style.

faqs.q: How long does Belfast sink installation take?
faqs.a: Fitting a Belfast sink takes longer than a standard sink — typically 2–4 hours for the unit preparation and sink fitting, not including plumbing connection.

title: How Much Does Howdens Kitchen Installation Cost?
metaDescription: Find out the typical cost to have a Howdens kitchen professionally installed. Labour rates, what's included and how to get an accurate quote.
answer: Installation of a Howdens kitchen typically costs £1,500–£3,500 depending on kitchen size and complexity. This is labour only, excluding the Howdens units, worktops and appliances.
bodyHtml:
What Affects the Cost

  • Number of units — more units mean more installation time
  • Worktop type — laminate is cut on site; stone worktops are fitted separately after templating
  • Integrated appliances — each integrated appliance adds fitting time
  • Old kitchen removal — typically £200–£400 additional if included
  • Complexity — corner units, island units, unusual room conditions all add time

How to Get an Accurate Quote

A pre-installation survey from a specialist kitchen fitter is the only way to get an accurate price. The fitter assesses your room conditions, cross-checks your Howdens plan and provides a fixed price covering the full scope of work. Estimates without a site visit are unreliable.

What a Professional Installation Includes

A comprehensive Howdens installation quote typically includes all base and wall unit fitting, door and drawer alignment, worktop cutting and fitting, plinth and cornice fitting, integrated appliance installation, and a final snagging check.

Cost Guide by Kitchen Size

Kitchen sizeUnitsDurationLabour guide
Small8–123–4 days£1,800–£2,800
Medium13–204–6 days£2,800–£4,200
Large21+6–10 days£4,200–£7,500

Howdens-Specific Installation Details

Howdens units use their own fixing rail and door adjustment hardware, which differs slightly from other rigid kitchen brands — a fitter who has worked with the system before will typically move through door and drawer alignment faster than one seeing it for the first time, which can make a genuine difference to the total number of days quoted.

Does Howdens Charge for a Design Survey?

Howdens' in-depot design consultation is separate from, and not a substitute for, an independent installation survey — the design consultation confirms the kitchen can be specified and ordered; it does not assess your room's structural or service conditions for fitting purposes.

faqs.q: Does Howdens offer installation?
faqs.a: Howdens is a trade-only supplier and does not offer a consumer installation service. You need to arrange your own independent kitchen fitter.

faqs.q: Can I get a cheaper installation for a Howdens kitchen?
faqs.a: Getting multiple fixed-price quotes after surveys is the best way to compare installation costs. The cheapest quote may not include all scope items — compare carefully.

faqs.q: Does Howdens kitchen installation include worktops?
faqs.a: The installation of worktops is separate from Howdens unit supply. If worktops are included in your installation quote, confirm exactly what is covered — fitting of laminate worktops differs from stone worktops, which require templating.

title: Can You Paint Kitchen Units Yourself?
metaDescription: Can you paint kitchen cabinet doors and units yourself? Find out how to do it properly and when to call a professional.
answer: Yes, kitchen units can be painted. It is possible to do it yourself but achieving a professional, durable result requires proper preparation, the right primer, and a kitchen-specific paint applied correctly. Many homeowners find a professional finish difficult to achieve without experience.
bodyHtml:
Can You DIY Paint Kitchen Units?

Yes, but the preparation is everything. Units must be fully degreased, sanded to provide a key, primed with the correct primer for the material (MDF, solid wood or vinyl-wrapped doors each require different primers) and painted in thin, even coats. Rushing the preparation produces a finish that chips and peels quickly.

Best Results: Spray Painting

A spray-painted finish gives the smoothest, most professional result on kitchen units. This is typically done by a professional kitchen painter using a spray gun. DIY brush and roller painting is possible but will show brush marks unless you use a very fine roller and finish with a tip-off brush technique.

When to Call a Professional

  • If your units are vinyl-wrapped — these require specific preparation and professional knowledge
  • If you want a factory-smooth finish without brush marks
  • If you have a large number of units and limited time

DIY Painting Step by Step

  1. Remove doors, drawer fronts and all handles/hinges
  2. Degrease thoroughly with sugar soap or a dedicated degreaser
  3. Sand to create a key — a fine-grit sanding sponge is usually sufficient
  4. Apply the correct primer for the substrate (MDF, wood or vinyl-wrapped)
  5. Apply two to three thin top coats, allowing full cure time between each
  6. Leave to cure fully, often 1–2 weeks, before rehanging doors

Substrate Matters More Than People Expect

Vinyl-wrapped (foil) doors need a specialist adhesion primer — standard wood primer will not bond properly and can peel within months. If you're not certain what your doors are made of, it's worth checking with the manufacturer or your original retailer before starting.

How Long Should You Wait Before Using a Painted Kitchen Normally?

Even when top coats feel dry to the touch within a day, most paints need one to two weeks to fully cure and reach their maximum hardness — avoid heavy use, wiping or knocks to freshly painted doors during this period.

faqs.q: What paint is best for kitchen units?
faqs.a: A hard-wearing water-based alkyd paint (such as Farrow and Ball full gloss or Rust-Oleum kitchen cupboard paint) works well. Always prime first with an appropriate primer for the substrate.

faqs.q: How long does painted kitchen unit paint last?
faqs.a: With proper preparation and a quality paint, a painted finish can last 5–10 years. High-traffic areas (around handles and near the sink) will show wear first.

faqs.q: Is painting kitchen units worth it?
faqs.a: Yes — painting is one of the most cost-effective ways to transform a kitchen. New doors or a full kitchen replacement cost significantly more.

title: What Is a Correlated Kitchen?
metaDescription: A correlated kitchen coordinates all elements — doors, handles, worktops and appliances — to a unified design scheme. Find out what this means in practice.
answer: A correlated kitchen is one where all design elements — cabinet colours, door profiles, worktop material, handle style and sometimes appliances — are coordinated to a unified scheme. It is a design approach rather than a specific product category.
bodyHtml:
What Correlation Means in Kitchen Design

In kitchen design, correlation refers to the deliberate matching or complementing of all visual elements. A correlated kitchen has a clear design logic: the door colour relates to the worktop; the handle style reflects the door profile; the appliance finish matches the colour scheme. Nothing is arbitrary.

How It Affects Installation

A highly correlated kitchen design places greater demands on installation precision. When every element is designed to work together, misalignment is more visible — gaps between doors that are slightly inconsistent, a worktop that is a fraction out of level, or a plinth that doesn't sit flat all stand out more than they would in a less cohesive design.

Achieving a Correlated Look

  • Start with a consistent door colour and profile as the anchor for all other decisions
  • Choose worktop material and colour in person, not from a screen
  • Select handles that suit the door profile — bar handles for handleless-adjacent styles, cup handles for shaker

Elements That Typically Need to Correlate

ElementShould relate to
Door colourWorktop tone and wall colour
Handle finishTap and appliance finish
Worktop materialSplashback and flooring
Appliance colour/finishOverall cabinetry scheme

A Practical Way to Test Correlation Before Ordering

Request physical samples of your door colour, worktop and flooring together in the room you're fitting the kitchen into, viewed in both daylight and evening light — showroom lighting can make colours look more coordinated than they will under your own kitchen's lighting.

Does Correlation Mean Everything Has to Match Exactly?

No — good correlation is about elements relating to each other deliberately, which can include intentional contrast, such as a dark island against light perimeter units, rather than every surface being an identical tone.

faqs.q: Is a correlated kitchen more expensive?
faqs.a: Not inherently. Correlation is a design principle, not a price point. You can achieve a well-coordinated kitchen at most budget levels with careful choices.

faqs.q: Does kitchen design correlation affect the fitter?
faqs.a: It places higher demands on installation quality — the fitter must achieve consistent door gaps, precise worktop joints and level plinths for the coordinated look to read correctly.

faqs.q: Do kitchen retailers offer correlated ranges?
faqs.a: Many do. Premium retailers like Magnet, Masterclass and German brands offer curated colour stories and accessory ranges designed to coordinate.

title: What Happens If a Kitchen Fitter Damages Something?
metaDescription: What are your rights if a kitchen fitter damages your property or kitchen during installation? Find out who is responsible and how to resolve it.
answer: If a kitchen fitter damages your property or kitchen units during installation, you are entitled to have the damage made good at the fitter's expense. A reputable fitter will have public liability insurance to cover accidental damage.
bodyHtml:
Your Rights

Under consumer law, if a tradesperson damages your property during the course of their work, they are responsible for repairing or replacing the damage. This applies whether the damage is to your property (walls, floors, existing fittings) or to items in their care (kitchen units, appliances).

What to Do If Damage Occurs

  • Document the damage immediately with photographs
  • Inform the kitchen fitter in writing (text or email creates a record)
  • Give the fitter the opportunity to rectify the problem before engaging other parties
  • If the fitter does not respond, contact their public liability insurer

Why Insurance Matters

A professional kitchen fitter should carry public liability insurance. This covers accidental damage to your property during their work. Always ask for proof of insurance before booking any tradesperson.

Steps to Take If Damage Occurs

  1. Photograph the damage immediately, before anything is moved or cleaned
  2. Notify the fitter in writing the same day
  3. Ask for their proposed remedy and timescale in writing
  4. If unresolved, request their public liability insurance details
  5. Escalate to the insurer directly if the fitter does not respond within a reasonable time

What Counts as Reasonable Wear vs Damage?

Minor marks from moving heavy items — a small scuff on a skirting board, for example — are generally considered reasonable and are usually made good as part of finishing, whereas a cracked tile, a hole in plasterboard or a damaged appliance is clearly beyond normal wear and should be treated as a damage claim.

Should You Get Everything in Writing Before Work Starts?

Yes — a written quote that references insurance cover, and photographs of the existing condition of anything valuable nearby, gives you a clear baseline if a dispute over damage ever arises.

faqs.q: Can I withhold payment if a kitchen fitter damages something?
faqs.a: You can reasonably withhold a portion of payment that corresponds to the cost of making good the damage. Take legal advice if the fitter disputes liability.

faqs.q: What if a kitchen unit is damaged during installation?
faqs.a: If a unit is damaged during installation, the fitter is responsible for replacement. Document the damage and report it to the fitter immediately.

faqs.q: Does a kitchen fitter's insurance cover damage to new kitchen units?
faqs.a: Public liability insurance covers accidental damage to client property. Whether units are covered depends on the specific policy — check with the insurer.

title: How Do You Level a Kitchen on a Sloping Floor?
metaDescription: Sloping floors are common in older UK homes. Find out how professional kitchen fitters level units on uneven or sloping floors.
answer: Kitchen units are levelled on sloping floors using adjustable plinth legs. Each leg can be individually raised or lowered to compensate for floor variation, achieving a perfectly level unit regardless of what the floor does.
bodyHtml:
Plinth Legs

Modern kitchen units are fitted on adjustable plastic plinth legs (typically 100–150mm tall) that can be screwed up or down. By adjusting each leg independently, the fitter can level a unit across a floor with significant slope — typically up to 60mm variation — without shimming or cutting.

The Levelling Process

The fitter uses a spirit level (or laser level for larger runs) to establish the highest point in the floor. All units are then set to this level, with the legs on the lower parts of the floor adjusted upwards to compensate. The plinth panels that run along the bottom of the unit run conceal the legs and any floor variation behind them.

When Floors Are Very Severely Sloped

  • If floor variation exceeds the leg adjustment range, a levelling screed or floor build-up may be required before installation
  • Wall unit height must also be adjusted if floor slope affects ceiling clearance at one end of the kitchen
  • A survey is essential for identifying severe floor conditions in advance

The Levelling Process Step by Step

  1. Establish the highest point of the floor across the kitchen footprint using a laser or spirit level
  2. Set the first unit at that highest point with legs at minimum extension
  3. Work outward, extending each subsequent unit's legs to match the reference height
  4. Check the full run is level along its length and depth before fixing to the wall
  5. Fit plinth panels to conceal the legs and any visible floor variation

What Happens at the Extremes of Leg Adjustment

If one end of the kitchen needs legs extended close to their maximum and the floor continues to drop beyond that point, additional packers or a localised screed patch may be needed rather than relying on the legs alone — this is exactly the kind of detail a pre-installation survey is designed to catch.

Does a Sloping Floor Affect Appliance Fitting?

It can — an integrated dishwasher or oven housing relies on the surrounding units being level for its door to close and align correctly, so any floor slope needs to be fully resolved by the unit levelling before appliances are fitted into their housings.

faqs.q: How much floor slope can kitchen units handle?
faqs.a: Standard plinth legs accommodate floor variation of up to 60mm. Beyond this, floor preparation (screed or battening) is usually required.

faqs.q: Will a sloping floor affect the cost of installation?
faqs.a: A moderately sloping floor adds adjustment time but not usually significant cost. A severely sloped floor that requires preparation work will add cost — this will be identified at survey.

faqs.q: Do sloping floors affect worktop fitting?
faqs.a: The worktop sits on the unit tops which are levelled independently of the floor. Once units are level, the worktop line is level regardless of floor slope.

title: What Is the Best Kitchen Brand in the UK?
metaDescription: Which is the best kitchen brand in the UK? From Wren and Howdens to Häcker and Neptune, find out how the top brands compare.
answer: The best kitchen brand depends on budget, design preference and how the kitchen will be used. Howdens and Wren dominate the mid-market; Häcker, Neptune and deVOL lead the premium market. All can be professionally installed to a high standard.
bodyHtml:
Mid-Market Leaders

Howdens is the UK's largest trade kitchen supplier, offering rigid units to trade customers through local depots. Wren is the largest consumer kitchen retailer, with showrooms nationally and a wide range of door styles. Both offer good quality for the price point.

Premium and Luxury Brands

Häcker (German) is widely regarded as the benchmark for precision-engineered, handleless kitchens. Neptune and deVOL offer high-quality British-designed kitchens in traditional and Shaker styles. Tom Howley and Harvey Jones produce bespoke in-frame kitchens at the top of the market.

What Matters Beyond Brand

  • The quality of the installation matters as much as the quality of the kitchen
  • A premium kitchen poorly fitted will not look or perform as it should
  • Choose a brand that suits your budget and appoint an experienced fitter with specific knowledge of that brand's system

Brand Comparison by Price Tier

TierBrandsKnown for
BudgetWickes, B&Q, IKEAValue, wide availability
Mid-marketHowdens, Wren, Magnet, SymphonyWide range, national coverage
Premium BritishNeptune, deVOL, Tom HowleyDesign-led, in-frame styles
Premium GermanHäcker, Nobilia, RotpunktPrecision manufacturing, handleless systems

Why the 'Best' Brand Question Has No Single Answer

A budget-conscious first-time buyer and someone specifying a kitchen for a long-term forever home are optimising for different things — cost and speed to fit versus longevity and finish precision — so the honest answer to 'what's the best brand' always depends on which of those two priorities matters more to you.

Does Brand Reputation Guarantee Installation Quality?

No — even the best-engineered kitchen brand will look poor if fitted by an inexperienced installer, and a modest brand fitted precisely by an experienced fitter often outperforms a premium brand fitted carelessly. The fitter matters as much as the brand.

faqs.q: Is Howdens better than Wren?
faqs.a: Howdens and Wren serve different markets. Howdens is trade-only and offers competitive pricing for rigid units; Wren is consumer-facing with an integrated showroom design service. Quality is comparable at similar price points.

faqs.q: Is a German kitchen worth the extra cost?
faqs.a: German kitchens (Häcker, Nobilia, Rotpunkt) typically offer superior unit construction tolerances and finish quality compared to mass-market UK alternatives. For many homeowners, the investment is justified by longevity and aesthetic precision.

faqs.q: What kitchen brand holds its value?
faqs.a: Premium kitchens from brands like Häcker, Neptune and deVOL hold their value better in property terms. A well-installed premium kitchen can add significant value to a home.

title: How Are Kitchen Appliances Measured for Fitting?
metaDescription: Kitchen appliances must be measured carefully to ensure they fit correctly into their housings. Find out how integrated appliances are measured and fitted.
answer: Kitchen appliances are measured by their standard niche dimensions — the space they need within the kitchen unit housing. Most integrated appliances are built to standard widths (450mm, 600mm) and heights (450mm, 820mm) that correspond to standard unit sizes.
bodyHtml:
Standard Appliance Dimensions

UK kitchen appliances are built to standard niche sizes. A standard dishwasher requires a 600mm wide by 820mm tall niche. A standard under-counter fridge requires a 600mm wide by 820mm tall niche. Built-in ovens typically require a 595mm wide by 590mm tall niche cut into a 600mm wide tower or base unit.

Checking Fit Before Installation

Your kitchen designer should specify the correct housing unit for each appliance in the plan. A pre-installation survey by your kitchen fitter will cross-check that the appliance dimensions match the specified housing and that the electrical supply point is in the correct position inside the housing.

What Goes Wrong When Measurements Are Wrong

  • An appliance that is slightly larger than the niche cannot be fitted without modification
  • A supply point in the wrong position inside a housing may prevent the appliance from sitting flush
  • Integrated doors that are the wrong height or offset will not align correctly

Standard Niche Sizes at a Glance

ApplianceStandard niche
Dishwasher600mm wide × 820mm tall
Under-counter fridge600mm wide × 820mm tall
Built-in single oven595mm wide × 590mm tall, in a 600mm tower/base unit
Washing machine600mm wide × 820mm tall

Why Manufacturer Variation Still Matters

Even within these standard niche sizes, individual manufacturers can vary by a few millimetres in depth or hinge clearance, which is usually fine but can occasionally cause a door to sit slightly proud or recessed compared to neighbouring units — checking the specific installation manual for your chosen model before ordering housing units avoids this.

What About Non-Standard or American-Style Appliances?

Larger appliances such as an American-style fridge-freezer or a range cooker don't follow the standard niche sizes at all and need bespoke housing dimensions confirmed at survey stage, ideally with the exact model already chosen rather than left as a placeholder in the plan.

faqs.q: What if my appliance doesn't fit the housing?
faqs.a: If an appliance is too large for its housing, either a different appliance must be sourced or the housing unit must be changed. This is why checking appliance specs against housing dimensions before ordering is essential.

faqs.q: Do all 600mm wide dishwashers fit the same housing?
faqs.a: Generally yes — 600mm wide dishwashers are designed to fit a standard 600mm housing. Minor variations in height exist between brands; check the exact niche requirement in the installation manual.

faqs.q: Who checks appliance measurements — the fitter or the designer?
faqs.a: The kitchen designer specifies housing units based on appliance selection. The kitchen fitter verifies this at survey and again on delivery. Both should check — errors caught early are far cheaper to correct.

title: What Glue Do Kitchen Fitters Use?
metaDescription: Find out what adhesives and glues professional kitchen fitters use for worktops, end panels, plinths and other kitchen installation tasks.
answer: Kitchen fitters use several types of adhesive depending on the task. Worktop joints use two-part polyester adhesive (Biscuit); end panels and plinths use general construction adhesive (e.g. No More Nails or Gripfill); silicone sealant is used for sink surrounds and worktop-wall junctions.
bodyHtml:
Worktop Joint Adhesive

Worktop joints — particularly for laminate worktops — are joined using a two-part polyester adhesive specifically designed for worktops (commonly known as 'Biscuit' after the colour). This sets hard, is water-resistant and fills any minor gap in the joint. Routed joints (where a curved jig is used to create a perfectly matched joint profile) use the same adhesive.

Panel and Plinth Adhesive

For fixing end panels, light pelmet and decorative elements, a solvent-based or water-based construction adhesive is used alongside mechanical fixings. Products like Gripfill, No More Nails or Stixall are common. These provide a strong bond while remaining flexible enough to accommodate minor movement.

Silicone Sealant

Silicone is used for finishing joints between the worktop and wall, around the sink (where it also provides a waterproof seal) and in any other junction where flexibility and waterproofing are needed. Kitchen-grade silicone is anti-fungal to resist mould in humid conditions.

Adhesive Quick Reference

TaskAdhesive type
Worktop jointsTwo-part polyester ('biscuit') adhesive
End panels and plinthsConstruction adhesive (Gripfill, No More Nails, Stixall) plus fixings
Sink surround and worktop-wall junctionKitchen-grade anti-fungal silicone
Upstand fixingSilicone or a dedicated flexible sealant

Why the Adhesive Choice Affects Longevity

Using a general-purpose silicone rather than a kitchen-specific anti-fungal grade around a sink is a common shortcut that leads to mould growth in the joint within a year or two, particularly in less ventilated kitchens — insisting on the correct kitchen-grade product is a small detail that materially affects how the finish looks over time.

Can Adhesive Fully Replace Mechanical Fixings?

No — even where adhesive is used for panels and trims, mechanical fixings (screws) are still used wherever a component needs to bear load or be removable for future maintenance. Adhesive alone is never used for structural connections in kitchen fitting.

faqs.q: Do kitchen fitters glue units to the wall?
faqs.a: Not typically. Units are mechanically fixed to the wall using screws. Adhesive alone is not used to fix units.

faqs.q: What adhesive is used for kitchen end panels?
faqs.a: Construction adhesive (Gripfill, No More Nails or similar) combined with small fixings is typically used for end panels. Silicone may be used for the final seal at the wall junction.

faqs.q: Can I use silicone instead of worktop adhesive?
faqs.a: No. Silicone does not provide the rigid, load-bearing bond needed for a worktop joint. Two-part polyester adhesive is the correct material for worktop joining.

title: What Is a Handleless Kitchen Rail System?
metaDescription: A handleless rail system replaces traditional handles with an integrated grip rail. Find out how it works and what it requires from installation.
answer: A handleless rail system (also called a J-rail or aluminium rail system) replaces traditional pull handles with a recessed metal rail integrated into the door or a strip fitted between the door and the unit. It gives a clean, handle-free appearance while maintaining grip for opening.
bodyHtml:
How Rail Systems Work

In a J-rail system, a metal profile (typically aluminium) is fitted along the top and bottom of each door. The profile creates a recessed grip area. The rail can be mounted on the door face (surface mounted) or integrated into the door edge profile. When you open a door, your fingers fit into the rail rather than gripping a separate handle.

Installation Requirements

  • Handleless rail systems demand extremely precise door alignment — gaps must be consistent to within 1mm for the rail lines to run visually true across the kitchen
  • The rail is fixed to the door and to the unit frame — both must be exactly aligned for the integrated look to work
  • Hinge selection and adjustment is critical — hinges must hold the door in exactly the right position without drift

Why It Demands a Skilled Fitter

A handleless kitchen with rail system is one of the most demanding types to install precisely. The absence of handles means every millimetre of misalignment is visible. An experienced kitchen fitter will spend significant time adjusting door positions to achieve consistent rail lines across the entire kitchen.

Surface-Mounted vs Integrated Rail Systems

Surface-mounted railIntegrated edge profile
Where it sitsFixed to the face of the doorMachined into the door edge itself
Retrofit potentialCan sometimes be added to existing doorsMust be specified when doors are manufactured
Visual effectVisible rail line across the runNear-invisible grip channel

Why Hinge Quality Matters More Than Usual Here

Because there's no handle to compensate for a door that's slightly out of alignment, handleless kitchens rely on higher-quality, more precisely adjustable hinges than a standard handled kitchen — cheaper hinge mechanisms tend to drift out of adjustment faster under daily use, which is far more noticeable on a handleless design.

Can a Handled Kitchen Be Converted to Handleless Later?

Generally no, not without replacing the doors — the rail or edge profile is part of the door manufacturing, so converting an existing handled kitchen means ordering new doors rather than modifying the existing ones.

faqs.q: Is a handleless kitchen harder to clean?
faqs.a: The recessed rail can collect grease and debris if not cleaned regularly. Wiping the inside of the rail as part of kitchen cleaning keeps it hygienic.

faqs.q: Does a handleless kitchen cost more to install?
faqs.a: Yes, typically — the precision required for consistent rail alignment adds installation time compared to a kitchen with traditional handles.

faqs.q: Which kitchen brands use rail systems?
faqs.a: Rail systems are used by most major handleless kitchen ranges including Wren's Infinity Plus, Howdens' Lincoln, Magnet's handleless ranges, and most German brands (Häcker, Nobilia, Rotpunkt).

title: Can Kitchen Units Be Reused?
metaDescription: Is it possible to reuse kitchen units after removal? Find out when reuse is practical and when replacement is the better option.
answer: Kitchen units can sometimes be reused, but it depends on their condition, the method of original installation and whether they can be safely removed without damage. Rigid pre-assembled units in good condition are the most likely candidates for reuse.
bodyHtml:
When Reuse Is Practical

Rigid kitchen units that were fitted with screws and are in good structural condition may be reusable. If the carcasse is sound, the hinge mounting positions are undamaged and the unit can be removed cleanly, it can be fitted in a new position. This is most common when rearranging a kitchen layout rather than a full replacement.

When Reuse Is Not Practical

  • Flatpack units (including IKEA) often cannot be disassembled and reassembled reliably — the joints weaken on removal
  • Units that were adhesive-bonded are unlikely to survive removal undamaged
  • Units with significant wear, water damage to the base or damaged hinge areas are not worth reusing
  • If the new layout requires different sizes, the existing units will not fit

New Doors on Old Units

A practical middle ground is to keep sound carcasses and fit new doors, drawer fronts and worktops. This can achieve a fresh kitchen look at significantly less cost than full replacement.

Reuse Decision Guide

ConditionRecommendation
Rigid, screw-fixed, no water damageGood candidate for reuse
Flatpack, previously assembledRisky — joints often weaken on disassembly
Adhesive-bonded constructionNot practical to reuse
Sound carcass, tired doorsKeep carcass, replace doors/worktop only

What a Fitter Checks Before Recommending Reuse

Beyond visible condition, a fitter will check that carcasses are still square, that hinge mounting points aren't stripped or enlarged from repeated adjustment, and that the base of each unit hasn't absorbed moisture from previous leaks — any of these issues can undermine the case for reuse even if a unit looks fine on the surface.

Is It Worth Paying to Have Units Assessed Before Deciding?

If you're on the fence, a short assessment as part of your pre-installation survey is far cheaper than committing to a reuse plan that then fails during installation, forcing a same-day decision to order replacements under time pressure.

faqs.q: Can I donate old kitchen units?
faqs.a: Yes. Many local charities and organisations such as Habitat for Humanity or local Facebook groups accept kitchen units in good condition.

faqs.q: Can a kitchen fitter advise on reuse?
faqs.a: Yes — a good kitchen fitter will assess the existing units at survey stage and tell you honestly whether reuse is viable and worthwhile.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to reuse kitchen units?
faqs.a: It can be — but only if the reused units are genuinely in good condition and the savings are not offset by additional fitting complexity.

title: How Do You Fit an Extractor Fan in a Kitchen?
metaDescription: How is a kitchen extractor fan installed? Find out what's involved in fitting a hood extractor, ceiling extractor or ducted extraction system.
answer: A kitchen extractor fan is fitted by securing the unit to a wall unit, island ceiling or dedicated mounting position, connecting it to a duct that exits through an external wall or roof, and wiring it to the electrical supply. Ducted extraction is preferred over recirculation for performance.
bodyHtml:
Types of Kitchen Extraction

Ducted extraction removes cooking fumes, steam and grease through a duct to the outside. It is the most effective system. Recirculation systems filter air through charcoal and return it to the room — no external duct is needed, but they are less effective at removing moisture and heat.

Installation Steps for a Ducted Extractor

  • Route the duct from the extractor position to an external exit point (usually through a wall behind the kitchen or upward through the ceiling)
  • Fit the duct grille on the external wall
  • Secure the extractor housing to the wall unit, ceiling or island support
  • Connect electrical supply (typically via a switched fused spur)
  • Connect the duct to the extractor

Who Does the Extractor Installation?

The kitchen fitter typically installs the extractor housing and duct within the kitchen. If the duct exits through an external wall, this element may require a builder or be done by the fitter if access allows. The electrical connection must be made by a qualified electrician.

Ducted vs Recirculating: Quick Comparison

DuctedRecirculating
EffectivenessRemoves fumes, steam and heat outsideFilters air, returns it to the room
Requires external wall or roof accessYesNo
Ongoing maintenanceOccasional duct/grille cleaningCharcoal filter replacement needed periodically
Best suited toMost housesFlats or rooms with no external wall access

Positioning the Duct Route Correctly

The shortest, straightest possible route from extractor to the outside wall gives the best performance — every 90-degree bend in ducting reduces airflow, so a route with two or three tight bends may need a more powerful fan to achieve the same real-world extraction as a short straight run.

What If the Only External Wall Is a Long Way From the Hob?

In kitchens where the hob sits in the centre of an island, a downdraft extractor built into the worktop next to the hob, ducted below floor level, is sometimes used instead of a conventional overhead hood — this is a specialist installation and should be planned at the design stage, not added afterwards.

faqs.q: Does a kitchen extractor need planning permission?
faqs.a: Not usually for a standard extraction to an external wall. Some installations (listed buildings, conservation areas, certain flat regulations) may require consent. Check with your local authority if in doubt.

faqs.q: How far can an extractor duct run?
faqs.a: Extractor ducts should be as short and straight as possible. Most extractor fans are rated for a maximum duct run of 3–6 metres with bends reducing effective extraction. Longer or more complex runs may require a higher-power fan.

faqs.q: Can an extractor fan be recirculating instead of ducted?
faqs.a: Yes, though performance is lower. Recirculating models are the only option where external extraction is not possible (e.g. in apartments or where the cooker is in the centre of a room with no nearby external wall).

title: What Is a Quartz Worktop?
metaDescription: Find out what a quartz worktop is, how it is made, and whether it is the right choice for your kitchen.
answer: A quartz worktop is an engineered stone surface made from approximately 90% natural quartz crystals bound with resins and pigments. It is non-porous, extremely hard-wearing and available in a wide range of colours and finishes.
bodyHtml:
How Quartz Worktops Are Made

Engineered quartz worktops are manufactured by combining ground quartz with polymer resins under high pressure. The result is a dense, non-porous surface that does not need sealing. Pigments are added during manufacturing to achieve consistent colour, making engineered quartz more predictable in appearance than natural granite.

Key Advantages

  • Non-porous — does not absorb liquids or stains
  • No sealing required
  • Consistent appearance (unlike natural stone where each slab is unique)
  • Extremely hard-wearing and scratch resistant
  • Hygienic and easy to clean

Limitations

  • Not suitable for outdoor use — UV exposure causes fading
  • Can be damaged by very high heat — use trivets or pan stands
  • Heavier than laminate, requiring strong unit tops
  • Cannot be cut on site — requires specialist templating and fabrication

Quartz vs Granite vs Laminate at a Glance

QuartzGraniteLaminate
PorosityNon-porousPorous, needs sealingNon-porous surface layer
Colour consistencyVery consistentUnique per slabVery consistent
Heat resistanceGood, avoid direct extreme heatVery highModerate, use trivets
Cut on site?No — factory cut from templateNo — factory cut from templateYes

What Affects Quartz Cost Most

Beyond the base price per linear metre, the biggest cost variables are slab colour (some patterns cost significantly more than plain colours), edge profile complexity, and the number of joints required — a kitchen with an island typically needs at least one additional joint compared to a straightforward run.

Can Quartz Be Installed Over Existing Units?

Yes, provided the existing units are level, sound and structurally capable of bearing the additional weight of a stone worktop compared to whatever was fitted previously — this should always be checked before committing to a quartz upgrade on an older kitchen.

faqs.q: Is quartz better than granite for a kitchen worktop?
faqs.a: Quartz is generally more practical — it requires no sealing, has consistent colour and is non-porous. Granite is natural stone with unique character but requires periodic sealing.

faqs.q: How much does a quartz worktop cost?
faqs.a: Quartz worktops typically cost £300–£900 per linear metre installed, depending on brand, thickness, edge profile and complexity.

faqs.q: Can quartz worktops be repaired if chipped?
faqs.a: Minor chips can be repaired using a colour-matched epoxy resin filler. Deep chips or cracks may require professional repair or section replacement.

title: How Do You Fit Kitchen Cabinets to Stud Walls?
metaDescription: Fitting kitchen cabinets to stud (plasterboard) walls requires the right fixings and technique. Find out how professional kitchen fitters do it.
answer: Kitchen cabinets are fitted to stud walls by locating the timber or metal studs using a stud finder, then fixing directly into the studs using appropriate screws. Where fixings cannot land in studs, specialist hollow wall anchors rated for the load are used.
bodyHtml:
Finding Studs

The first step is to locate the wall studs using an electronic stud finder. Studs in UK timber-frame walls are typically spaced at 400mm or 600mm centres. Once located, fixings can be driven directly through the plasterboard and into the stud for a secure, load-bearing connection.

When Studs Are Not in the Right Position

Wall units must be fixed at specific heights and positions to align with the kitchen plan. If a stud does not fall where a fixing is needed, the options are: (a) use a hollow wall anchor rated for the required load, (b) fit a horizontal batten across two or more studs and fix the unit to the batten, or (c) fit a full-width plywood backer panel behind the wall units.

Metal Stud Walls

Metal stud partitions are common in modern builds and some older properties. Fixings into metal studs require self-tapping screws and must be located precisely on the stud centre. Load capacity is limited compared to timber studs — heavy units may require a plywood backer for adequate support.

Fixing Options When Studs Don't Line Up

OptionBest for
Hollow wall anchor rated for the loadLight to medium wall units, occasional off-stud fixing
Horizontal batten across studsA full run of units needing a continuous fixing line
Plywood backer panelHeavy units or metal stud walls with limited load capacity

Why Stud Spacing Catches People Out

UK timber stud walls are typically built to 400mm or 600mm centres, but older or non-standard builds can vary — a fitter who assumes standard spacing without checking can end up drilling test holes in the wrong places, which is why an electronic stud finder, not guesswork or knocking, is standard practice before any fixing begins.

Is a Plywood Backer Panel Visible Once the Kitchen Is Finished?

No — it sits behind the plasterboard or is fitted flush within the wall build-up before decoration, so it adds no visible thickness to the finished wall once the kitchen units are hung in front of it.

faqs.q: Can kitchen wall units be hung on plasterboard without studs?
faqs.a: Only with specialist hollow wall anchors rated for the load. Standard plasterboard fixings are not suitable for kitchen wall units. A professional will always try to fix into studs or use a batten system.

faqs.q: How much weight can a kitchen wall unit hold on a stud wall?
faqs.a: With fixings into timber studs, kitchen wall units can typically carry 50–100kg per cabinet. Hollow wall fixings carry less — always check the load rating against the anticipated cabinet weight.

faqs.q: Do I need to tell my kitchen fitter what type of wall I have?
faqs.a: It helps. Your kitchen fitter will establish wall construction at survey stage. Knowing in advance that you have stud walls allows them to plan fixings and bring appropriate equipment.

title: What Is a Pull-Out Kitchen Bin?
metaDescription: Pull-out kitchen bins are integrated waste solutions fitted inside kitchen cabinets. Find out how they work and how they are installed.
answer: A pull-out kitchen bin is a bin system built into a kitchen base unit that pulls out on a runner, typically attached to the door so it opens when you open the door. It conceals waste bins within the kitchen cabinetry for a tidy appearance.
bodyHtml:
How Pull-Out Bins Work

A pull-out bin unit consists of one or more bin containers mounted on a sliding frame inside a dedicated base cabinet. The door of the unit is either connected to the bin frame (so opening the door pulls out the bin automatically) or opens separately while the bin slides independently. Systems with door-linked pull-out action are the most popular as they require only one hand to operate.

Sizing and Cabinet Requirements

Pull-out bin systems are available in a range of widths — typically 300mm, 400mm, 450mm and 600mm. The system must be specified to match the available cabinet width. Some systems fit inside a single-door base unit; others require a wider two-door cabinet.

Installation Notes

  • The bin frame is fixed inside the base unit before the kitchen is installed, or as part of the kitchen fit
  • The door must be properly connected to the bin frame for the door-linked action to work
  • Once installed, door adjustment may be needed to ensure smooth, level operation

Sizing Guide

Cabinet widthTypical bin capacity
300mmSingle bin, around 15–20 litres
400mmSingle larger bin or two smaller bins
450–600mmTwo to three bins for waste and recycling separation

Door-Linked vs Independent Opening

Door-linked systems, where opening the cabinet door automatically pulls the bin frame out, are the most convenient for everyday use but need precise fixing between the door and the bin frame — if this connection is even slightly misaligned, the door can bind or the bin can drag on the cabinet sides, so this is worth checking carefully during snagging.

Can a Pull-Out Bin Go Under the Sink?

It can, but plumbing pipework under the sink often reduces the usable width, so a bin system for this position needs to be chosen to fit around the pipe runs — measure the actual clear space with pipework in place, not just the cabinet's nominal width.

faqs.q: Can a pull-out bin be added to an existing kitchen?
faqs.a: Yes, if you have a suitably sized base unit. Pull-out bin systems are available as retrofit kits for units from 300mm wide upward.

faqs.q: How many bins fit in a pull-out unit?
faqs.a: Typically 1–3 bins depending on the system width. A 600mm wide system can accommodate a main waste bin and one or two recycling bins.

faqs.q: Are pull-out bins easy to clean?
faqs.a: Yes — the bin containers lift out for washing. The runners and frame can be wiped down with the unit open. Liner bags help keep the bins clean.

title: How Much Does German Kitchen Installation Cost?
metaDescription: German kitchen installation typically costs more than standard UK kitchen fitting due to precision requirements. Find out typical costs and what is included.
answer: Installing a German kitchen (Häcker, Nobilia, Rotpunkt, Pronorm) typically costs £2,500–£5,000 in labour, depending on the kitchen size and complexity. The precision demands of German kitchen systems add time and skill requirements compared to standard UK kitchen installation.
bodyHtml:
Why German Kitchen Installation Costs More

German kitchen brands — particularly Häcker — specify gap tolerances of 0.5mm between door faces. Achieving and maintaining this requires more time in adjustment, a more experienced fitter, and careful management of the installation environment (temperature and humidity affect engineered wood components). The result, when achieved, is visually exceptional — but it requires patience and precision that not every fitter can deliver.

What Affects the Cost

  • Number of units — larger kitchens take proportionally longer
  • Door type — handleless systems with rail profiles require more alignment time than handled doors
  • Worktop type — stone worktops add a template visit and separate fitting day
  • Appliance integration — German kitchens typically have more integrated appliances than standard UK kitchens

How to Find a Fitter for a German Kitchen

Ask the German kitchen supplier for recommended installers, or seek a kitchen fitter with verified experience with the specific brand. A fitter experienced in Häcker, for example, will know the unit assembly system, the hanging rail method and the adjustment mechanisms specific to that brand.

Cost Guide by Kitchen Size

Kitchen sizeUnitsDurationLabour guide
Small8–123–4 days£1,800–£2,800
Medium13–204–6 days£2,800–£4,200
Large21+6–10 days£4,200–£7,500

German kitchens with handleless rail systems or very tight door tolerances often sit toward the upper end of these ranges even at a moderate unit count, because achieving the specified gap tolerances takes proportionally more adjustment time than a standard UK kitchen of the same size.

What Sets German Kitchen Installation Apart Day to Day

Fitters working on German systems typically spend more time on incremental hinge and gap adjustment throughout the install rather than at the end — small corrections are made continuously as each unit goes in, rather than left as a single snagging pass at completion.

Does Humidity or Temperature Affect Installation?

Engineered wood components used in some German kitchen ranges can be sensitive to significant swings in humidity during fitting — a newly plastered room that hasn't fully dried out, for example, is worth flagging to your fitter before installation begins.

faqs.q: Does Häcker install their own kitchens?
faqs.a: Häcker and most German kitchen brands supply through approved UK retailers who arrange installation. Häcker does not directly employ fitters in the UK.

faqs.q: Is a German kitchen worth the investment?
faqs.a: For homeowners who value precision, longevity and design quality, yes. German kitchens typically use higher-grade materials and tighter manufacturing tolerances than mass-market UK alternatives.

faqs.q: Can any kitchen fitter install a German kitchen?
faqs.a: Technically yes, but achieving the specified gap tolerances and finish quality requires experience with the specific brand's unit system. Using an experienced fitter makes a significant difference to the final result.
